_help: Ivy League local flavor for team pages, edition fronts and game write-ups. Same knobs as data/flavor.json (see FLAVOR_HELP in mac/gamer.py). Notes are fact-checked against the source URL each carries.

home_lines.text: Brown's Pizzitola Sports Center opened in February 1989 at a cost of $7.6 million, replacing Marvel Gymnasium, which stood next to Brown Stadium.
The Pizzitola Sports Center is named for Paul Bailey Pizzitola of Brown's class of 1981, whose father gave $2 million toward its construction.
Brown students call the Pizzitola Sports Center 'the Pitz,' and the 2,800-seat building also houses Brown volleyball, gymnastics, wrestling and squash.
The lobby of Brown's Pizzitola Sports Center honors John Heisman, and a 'TICKETS' sign salvaged from old Marvel Gymnasium is installed at the ticket window.

lines.text: Providence was settled in June 1636 by Roger Williams, who named the place in honor of 'God's merciful Providence.'
In 1772 a group from Providence burned the British customs schooner Gaspee south of the city, more than a year before the Boston Tea Party.
Providence grew on textiles and then on machine tools, jewelry and silverware, and in the 1960s trade magazines called the city 'the jewelry capital of the world.'
The dome of the Rhode Island State House in Providence is the fourth-largest self-supporting marble dome in the world.
The Providence Athenaeum, on Benefit Street on Brown's home turf of College Hill, is the fourth-oldest library in America.
Brown was founded on September 15, 1764, as Rhode Island College at the site of the First Baptist Church in Warren, and moved to Providence in 1770.
Rhode Island College offered its naming rights for a $5,000 gift in 1803, and Nicholas Brown Jr. answered the appeal the following year, giving Brown University its name.

At Brown the central Van Wickle Gate opens inward for new students at Convocation and outward for graduates at Commencement; a superstition holds that passing through it a second time too early means not graduating.
Brown played in the inaugural NCAA tournament in 1939, losing 42-30 to Villanova in the quarterfinals.
Brown won the Ivy League regular-season title in 1986 and returned to the NCAA tournament, where Syracuse beat the Bears 101-52 in the first round.
Brown's only appearance in the NIT came in 2003, when the Bears lost 89-73 to Virginia in the first round.
Brown beat UAB 83-78 in the 2019 College Basketball Invitational before falling 83-61 to Loyola Marymount in the next round.
Eric Reveno is Brown's men's basketball head coach for the 2026-27 season, according to the Brown athletics website.
Charles Evans Hughes graduated from Brown third in his class at 19 and later served as governor of New York, secretary of state and chief justice.
Janet Yellen graduated summa cum laude from Brown in 1967 and became the first woman to chair the Federal Reserve and the first woman to lead the Treasury.

home_lines.text: Columbia's Levien Gymnasium was completed on December 7, 1974, after construction began on August 1, 1972, as part of the Marcellus Hartley Dodge Physical Fitness Center.
Levien Gymnasium at Columbia is named for Francis S. Levien, a New York lawyer and industrialist who lived from 1905 to 1995.
The playing court inside Columbia's Levien Gymnasium is named for Jonathan D. Schiller, a former Columbia basketball player and university trustee.
Columbia's Levien Gymnasium hosted the 2016 CollegeInsider.com Postseason Tournament championship game and both the men's and women's 2024 Ivy League basketball tournaments.

lines.text: The Battle of Harlem Heights was fought in Morningside Heights on September 16, 1776, and a plaque by the Columbia gate at 117th Street and Broadway marks it.
Before Columbia arrived, Morningside Heights was home to the Bloomingdale Insane Asylum, which opened in 1821 and moved to suburban Westchester County in 1888.
Projects including a cathedral, St. Luke's Hospital and the Woman's Hospital led to Morningside Heights, the Manhattan neighborhood around Columbia, being known as an 'Academic Acropolis.'
Tom's Restaurant, on Broadway at 112th Street in Morningside Heights, was featured in the 1980s song 'Tom's Diner' and stood in for the diner on Seinfeld.
Grant's Tomb, the mausoleum of President Ulysses S. Grant, sits in the middle of Riverside Drive at 122nd Street in Morningside Heights.
Columbia was founded on October 31, 1754, as King's College by royal charter of George II, and the state legislature renamed it Columbia College in 1784.
Columbia moved to Morningside Heights in 1896 under president Seth Low, leaving 49th Street and Madison Avenue and taking the name Columbia University.
Daniel Chester French's Alma Mater statue sits on the steps of Low Memorial Library, the centerpiece of the Columbia campus and a National Historic Landmark.
The Helms Athletic Foundation listed Columbia as national champions for 1904, 1905 and 1910, unofficial selections the NCAA does not recognize as titles.
Columbia reached the NCAA tournament in 1948 and lost 76-53 to Kentucky in the regional semifinal before falling to Michigan in the third-place game.
Columbia's 1968 NCAA tournament team beat La Salle 83-69, lost 61-59 to Davidson in the regional semifinal and beat St. Bonaventure 95-75 for third place.
Columbia won the CollegeInsider.com Postseason Tournament in 2016, two years after an earlier appearance in the same event in 2014.
Jim McMillian led Columbia to a 63-14 record from 1967 to 1970, was a three-time All-American and later won the 1972 NBA title with the Lakers.
Barack Obama transferred to Columbia as a junior in 1981, lived off campus on West 109th Street and earned his bachelor's degree in 1983.

home_lines.text: Newman Arena opened in January 1990 inside Bartels Hall, the Cornell building that stands next to Lynah Rink on the Ithaca campus.
Cornell's Newman Arena is named for the late Floyd R. Newman, a member of the Class of 1912 and a major benefactor to the university.
Newman Arena replaced Barton Hall as Cornell's basketball home in Ithaca, and Barton Hall was remodeled to become a full-time indoor track venue for the university.

lines.text: Ithaca sits on the southern shore of Cayuga Lake in the Finger Lakes region, and its streams carved the gorges, rapids and waterfalls the area is known for.
Ithaca takes its name from the Greek island home of Ulysses, a name chosen by surveyor Simeon De Witt or his clerk, Robert Harpur.
Ithaca claims the ice cream sundae, first served in 1892 by fountain shop owner Chester Platt, though Two Rivers, Wisconsin, has long disputed the claim.
Moosewood Restaurant in Ithaca was founded as a collective in 1973 and went on to publish a number of vegetarian cookbooks.
During the early 20th century Ithaca was an important center of the silent film industry, until production centralized in Hollywood and work in Ithaca effectively ceased.
Cornell University was founded on April 27, 1865, by Ezra Cornell and Andrew Dickson White, both New York state senators at the time.
Cornell's unofficial mascot in Ithaca is a bear, a tradition dating to Touchdown, a live bear introduced in 1915.
Cornell's Dragon Day, founded in 1901 and held near St. Patrick's Day, has first-year architecture students build a dragon and parade it around central campus.
Cornell played its first basketball game on December 13, 1898, a 48-12 victory over the Waverly YMCA, and finished that short season 1-3.
From February 16, 1919, Cornell basketball played its home games in Barton Hall, which was first known simply as the New Armory.
In the 2010 NCAA tournament, 12th-seeded Cornell beat Temple 78-65 and Wisconsin 87-69 before losing to top-seeded Kentucky 62-45 in the Sweet Sixteen.
Cornell's 78-65 win over Temple in 2010 was the first NCAA tournament victory in the history of the Big Red men's basketball program.
Jon Jaques, a Cornell graduate of the Class of 2010, is the Robert E. Gallagher '44 Head Coach of Men's Basketball at Cornell.
Janet Reno enrolled at Cornell in 1956 and majored in chemistry, and in 1993 she became the first woman to serve as U.S. Attorney General.

home_lines.text: Leede Arena, a 2,100-seat venue in Hanover, was dedicated on May 22, 1987, and has been home to Dartmouth's men's and women's basketball teams since.
Dartmouth's Leede Arena honors Edward Leede, a 1949 graduate who was one of the school's leading basketball scorers.
Leede Arena sits inside the John W. Berry Sports Center in Hanover and was built to replace the old Alumni Gym next door.
Leede Arena in Hanover hosts the nation's longest-running women's basketball tournament and staged its 34th edition, the Blue Sky Classic, in 2010.

lines.text: Hanover was chartered by Governor Benning Wentworth on July 4, 1761, and its first European settlers, mostly from Connecticut, arrived in 1765 and 1766.
Hanover lies along the Connecticut River in Grafton County, New Hampshire, and the Appalachian Trail crosses the town on its way north.
In the 1780s Dresden, the southwest corner of Hanover around the Plain, briefly defected to the Vermont Republic before returning to New Hampshire at George Washington's heated insistence.
Hanover and Norwich, Vermont, share the Dresden School District, the first and one of the few interstate school districts in the nation.
The 1939 film Winter Carnival was shot in Hanover, the New Hampshire town that has been home to Dartmouth College since 1769.
Dartmouth was established by a royal charter issued on December 13, 1769, in the name of King George III, with Eleazar Wheelock as its founder.
Dartmouth's Big Green nickname dates to the 1860s, after students adopted Dartmouth Green as the college's official color in 1866.
Dartmouth's Winter Carnival was started in 1911 by the Dartmouth Outing Club to promote winter sports in Hanover.
Dartmouth reached the NCAA championship game in 1942 and lost to Stanford 53-38, the first of two title-game appearances for the Big Green.
Dartmouth returned to the NCAA championship game in 1944 and lost to Utah 42-40 in overtime.
Dartmouth made seven NCAA tournament appearances between 1941 and 1959, and the Big Green have an overall tournament record of 10-7.
Brett MacConnell is Dartmouth's men's basketball head coach, hired in 2026 after spending the 2025-26 season as an assistant coach at Stanford.

Daniel Webster graduated from Dartmouth in 1801 and later argued the college's side in Dartmouth College v. Woodward, where the Marshall Court ruled for Dartmouth against the New Hampshire legislature.

home_lines.text: Harvard's Lavietes Pavilion opened in 1926 and was originally the Briggs Athletic Center, named for LeBaron Russell Briggs, a Harvard College dean who also served as NCAA president.
Before Harvard basketball moved in, the Briggs building in Allston held an indoor track and batting cages that drew local baseball players, Ted Williams among them.
Harvard's men played their first game at what is now Lavietes Pavilion in November 1982, against neighbor and rival MIT, a day after the women's opener against Chicago.
In March 1996 Harvard rededicated its Allston gym to Ray Lavietes '36, a two-time basketball letterman whose $2.1 million gift funded a refurbishment.
With 1,636 seats, Harvard's Lavietes Pavilion is the smallest basketball arena in the Ivy League and the second-oldest college basketball arena still in use, behind Fordham's Rose Hill Gymnasium.

lines.text: Cambridge was founded in December 1630 as Newtowne, and the settlement was later renamed Cambridge in honor of the University of Cambridge in England.
George Washington arrived in Cambridge in July 1775 and took command of the Patriot soldiers camped on Cambridge Common.
Cambridge was home to more than 250 biotech companies in 2022, with over 120 of them in the Kendall Square ZIP code alone.
Allston, the Boston neighborhood that is home to Harvard's Lavietes Pavilion and is bordered by the Charles River, is named for the American painter and poet Washington Allston.
Allston was long a rail and livestock district, with a major Boston and Albany Railroad yard and stockyards and an abattoir nearby in northern Brighton.
Harvard was founded in 1636 by a vote of the Great and General Court of the Massachusetts Bay Colony and is the oldest institution of higher learning in the United States.
Harvard College took its name in 1639 from the clergyman John Harvard, who bequeathed the young school 780 pounds and a library of some 320 volumes.
Harvard students debuted the Harvard Turkey as the school's first unofficial mascot at the 2022 Harvard-Yale football game.
Harvard reached the 1946 NCAA tournament and lost 46-38 to Ohio State, and the Crimson then went 66 years before returning to the field in 2012.
Harvard's share of the 2010-11 Ivy League title was the program's first men's basketball Ivy championship since the league formed in the 1956-57 season.
In the 2014 NCAA tournament Harvard upset fifth-seeded Cincinnati 61-57 before falling to fourth-seeded Michigan State 80-73 in the round of 32.
Tommy Amaker was named Harvard's men's basketball coach on April 11, 2007, and in January 2009 his team beat Boston College for the program's first win over a ranked opponent.
Harvard's Ivy rivalry with Yale reached a pitch in 2015, when the Crimson beat the Bulldogs 53-51 in a playoff at the Palestra for the NCAA bid.
Tommy Amaker, Harvard's men's basketball head coach, enters his 20th season in Cambridge in 2026-27, with home games again at Lavietes Pavilion.
Jeremy Lin earned an economics degree from Harvard in 2010 as a unanimous first-team All-Ivy pick and later became the first Asian American player to win an NBA championship.

home_lines.text: Penn's Palestra opened on January 1, 1927, seating about 10,000 at first, and now holds 8,725 for basketball in Philadelphia.
The Palestra was designed by Charles Klauder and named by Penn Greek professor William N. Bates for the palaestra, an ancient enclosure where athletes competed before spectators.
Penn's Palestra, called the Cathedral of College Basketball, has hosted more games, more visiting teams and more NCAA tournaments than any other facility in college basketball.
Philadelphia's Big 5 originally played all of its games at Penn's Palestra, which also hosted the inaugural Ivy League men's and women's tournaments in 2017.
The Palestra was set as the site of the 2027 Ivy League Tournament, on March 12 and 13, in celebration of the Philadelphia arena's 100th anniversary.

lines.text: The name University City was coined in the mid-1950s by two realtors who were Penn graduates, hoping to draw Penn faculty back to the neighborhoods near the Penn campus.
Much of the University City area colloquially known as the Black Bottom, around Greenville, was destroyed under a 1960s gentrification plan in West Philadelphia.
University City sits directly across the Schuylkill River from Center City Philadelphia and holds 30th Street Station, one of the nation's busiest passenger train stations.
Andrew Hamilton bought land in 1735, and the area that is now part of Philadelphia's University City came to be known as Hamilton Village.
The Woodlands estate in University City once held a sprawling botanical garden and mansion, and its gardens in West Philadelphia are now the Woodlands Cemetery.
The University of Pennsylvania officially dates its founding to 1740, a date its trustees adopted in 1899, though Penn's archivist has cited other possible founding years.
Penn's medical school, opened in 1765, is described as the first medical school in America, and Penn's Latin motto translates as 'Laws without morals are useless.'
The Penn Relays have been held at Franklin Field since 1895 and are the oldest and largest track-and-field competition in the United States.
The Helms Athletic Foundation retroactively named Penn the national champion for 1919-20 and 1920-21, titles the NCAA does not officially recognize.
Led by Tony Price, Penn reached the 1979 Final Four in Salt Lake City by beating Iona, North Carolina, Syracuse and St. John's.
Penn lost the 1979 national semifinal 101-67 to a Michigan State team featuring Earvin 'Magic' Johnson, then fell 96-93 to DePaul in the third-place game.
Penn's 1979 team remains the last Ivy League team to reach the Final Four and the Elite Eight, and the Quakers are members of Philadelphia's Big 5.
Penn's main Ivy League basketball rival is Princeton, and the two schools used to always meet in the last game of the regular season.
Fran McCaffery leads Penn into the 2026-27 season and announced the Quakers' Ivy League schedule in August 2026, ahead of the Palestra's 100th anniversary.

home_lines.text: Princeton's Jadwin Gymnasium hosted the Tigers for the first time on January 25, 1969, and has been their home court ever since.
Jadwin Gymnasium in Princeton was designed by Walker O. Cain and is known for a roof made of three interlocking shells.

Princeton's Jadwin Gymnasium is named for Leander Stockwell Jadwin, class of 1928, a track captain who died months after graduating; the university put $6.5 million of his mother's $27 million gift toward it.
Jadwin Gymnasium holds 250,000 square feet of floor space on five levels and hosted first-round NCAA men's basketball tournament games in Princeton in 1970 and 1972.

lines.text: Henry Greenland, who built a house in 1683, was the first European to make his home within the bounds of present-day Princeton, where the Lenape were the earliest identifiable inhabitants.
The name Princeton first appeared in 1724 and is said to honor Prince William of Orange, though no documentary evidence confirms the story.
General Hugh Mercer was mortally wounded at the Battle of Princeton on January 3, 1777, a pivotal victory for George Washington.
Princeton's separate borough and township merged after a 2011 vote, with the consolidation taking effect on January 1, 2013.
Albert Einstein, the physicist who lived from 1879 to 1955, was a fellow at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey.
Princeton University was founded in 1746 in Elizabeth as the College of New Jersey, moved to Newark, and settled in Princeton in 1756.
Princeton's Nassau Hall served as the seat of the Congress of the Confederation from June 30 to November 4, 1783, making it the capitol of the United States.
Two bronze tigers have flanked the front entrance of Princeton's Nassau Hall since 1911, standing watch for the school's Tigers.
Princeton reached the 1965 Final Four, and Bill Bradley was named the tournament's Most Outstanding Player as the Tigers finished third.
Pete Carril coached Princeton from 1967 to 1996, going 514-261 and winning or sharing 13 Ivy League championships with the Princeton offense.
In 1996 Princeton beat defending national champion UCLA 43-41 in the first round of the NCAA tournament, Pete Carril's final college victory.
As a 15th seed in 2023, Princeton beat Arizona 59-55 and Missouri 78-63 to reach the Sweet 16, where Creighton won 86-75.
Princeton's 16th-seeded team lost 50-49 to Georgetown in the first round of the 1989 NCAA tournament.
Mitch Henderson enters his 15th season as Princeton's men's basketball head coach in 2026-27, according to the Princeton athletics website.
Bill Bradley scored 2,503 points at Princeton, won NBA titles with the Knicks in 1970 and 1973, and served New Jersey as a U.S. senator from 1979 to 1997.

home_lines.text: Yale plays in John J. Lee Amphitheater inside Payne Whitney Gymnasium, which opened in New Haven in 1932 to a design by John Russell Pope.
Yale's Payne Whitney Gymnasium, known as the cathedral of sweat for its Gothic Revival style, is called the second-largest gym in the world by cubic feet.
John Hay Whitney gave Yale its New Haven gymnasium in honor of his father, Payne Whitney, and the building rises to a nine-story tower.
Yale's 2,532-seat basketball arena was named in 1996 for John J. Lee, a former Yale basketball star and benefactor of the university.

lines.text: New Haven was founded in 1638 when about 500 Puritans led by Reverend John Davenport and merchant Theophilus Eaton sailed into the harbor.
New Haven was laid out on a Nine Square Plan around a central common, now the 16-acre Green at the heart of downtown.
New Haven shared the role of Connecticut's capital from 1701 until 1873, and the Amistad mutineers were tried in its federal court in 1839.
New Haven-style pizza, known locally as apizza, debuted at Frank Pepe Pizzeria Napoletana in 1925.
The regicides Edward Whalley and William Goffe, who signed the death warrant of Charles I, hid at West Rock in New Haven with John Davenport's help.
Yale began as the Collegiate School, established by an act of Connecticut's General Court in 1701, and its trustees voted in 1716 to move it to New Haven.
The Collegiate School became Yale College in 1718 on Cotton Mather's suggestion; Elihu Yale had donated nine bales of goods that sold for more than 560 pounds.
Yale's bulldog mascot, Handsome Dan, began with a dog bought by Yale student Andrew Barbey Graves, and Handsome Dan XIX was announced as mascot in 2021.
Penn and Yale played the first college basketball game with five men on a team in 1897, a year after Yale's first basketball season.
The Helms Athletic Foundation named Yale the national champion in 1901 and 1903, early in the life of the New Haven program.
Yale won its first NCAA tournament game in 2016, beating Baylor 79-75 in the first round.
As a No. 13 seed and a 13.5-point underdog in 2024, Yale beat fourth-seeded Auburn 78-76 in the NCAA tournament.
James Jones, the Joel E. Smilow '54 Head Coach of Men's Basketball and Yale's all-time winningest coach, leads the Bulldogs again in 2026-27.
Chris Dudley played at Yale from 1983 to 1987, spent 16 seasons in the NBA, and was Oregon's Republican nominee for governor in 2010.
Harvard and Yale tied for the 2015 Ivy League title, and Harvard won the playoff 53-51 at the Palestra, keeping Yale out of the NCAA tournament.
Yale beat Harvard 97-85 in 2019 to win its first Ivy League men's basketball tournament.
Yale and Harvard tied for the 2015 Ivy League title, and Harvard won the playoff 53-51 at the Palestra, keeping Yale out of the NCAA tournament.
Penn and Princeton play what the Daily Pennsylvanian calls the third-oldest rivalry in the sport, a series in which each side has won more than 120 games.
Princeton took the all-time series lead over Penn for the first time with a comeback win on January 5, 2026, in a game Penn had led by 13 points.
Princeton and Penn play what the Daily Pennsylvanian calls the third-oldest rivalry in the sport, a series in which each side has won more than 120 games.
Princeton's comeback win over Penn on January 5, 2026, gave the Tigers the all-time series lead for the first time, after Penn had led that game by 13 points.
